blocks.text: Count executions of the scan body. The first pass visits n elements and the second pass visits another n, for 2n visits. Big-O describes how that count grows as n grows: multiplying n by the constant 2 does not change the growth class, so the tight asymptotic bound is Θ(n), commonly written O(n). Multiplication would be justified only if one full scan happened inside every iteration of the other.

blocks.alt: Two sequential rows of work are added as n plus n, while a nested grid repeats n units for each of n rows and therefore multiplies to n squared.

The body being short affects only a constant factor; it does not remove repetitions. By contrast, two loops that run consecutively would add their costs instead of multiplying them.

Dividing by 2 changes only a constant factor, while the n² term remains, so the running time is Θ(n²). A shrinking inner loop is not automatically linear; you must add all of its lengths.

blocks.text: Write out the sequence: n, n/2, n/4, n/8, and so on. After k halvings the value is n/2^k. The loop ends once that value is below 1, which is equivalent to 2^k being at least n. Solving for k gives log₂ n. The important signal is multiplicative shrinkage: subtracting one would take linear time, but repeatedly dividing by a fixed factor takes logarithmic time.

blocks.text: Do not count the inner loop as n for every outer iteration unless it restarts. Instead, charge each iteration to a pointer advance. A left pointer can advance at most n positions and a right-moving pointer can also advance at most n positions, so there are at most 2n advances. If every loop iteration makes at least one such advance, there can be only O(n) iterations overall. This aggregate argument fails if an inner pointer resets and revisits the same elements for every outer iteration.

messages.text: O(1) work per iteration still accumulates across at most 2n pointer-advancing iterations, giving O(n).
Nested loops can be quadratic when inner work resets.
Names such as `left` and `right` provide no bound unless their movement and reset behavior are proved.

blocks.text: Complexity comes from a count, not from a naming convention. Inspect the initial value, update rule, stopping condition, and work per iteration. For example, `i += 1` from 0 to n performs about n iterations, while `i *= 2` from 1 to n performs about log n; both variables may be named i. A nested loop can also reset i and make the total quadratic. Derive the bound from behavior.

blocks.text: Use the rules in order. Count each phase, add phases that run one after another, and multiply only when one count repeats fully for every execution of another. Once you have an expression such as 3n² + 5n, constants and lower-order terms can be removed for the asymptotic class, yielding Θ(n²). Variable names are never an input to this calculation; they do not change how often the program runs.

blocks.text: Ask whether an element can be charged only a constant number of times. A monotonic inner pointer never returns to an earlier element, so all of its advances together are bounded by n. Likewise, an item pushed once and popped once contributes at most two stack operations. A full inner scan that resets to the beginning for every outer iteration has no such shared bound: it performs n work n times, or Θ(n²).

messages.text: Restarting a full n-element scan for every one of n outer iterations performs n · n = n² work.
Charging each element only a constant number of inner-body executions bounds their aggregate by O(n).
One push and at most one later pop per item gives at most 2n stack operations overall.
A monotonic pointer crosses at most n positions across all outer iterations because it never resets.

blocks.text: These facts form a recurrence such as T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. The number of children controls branching, child size controls recursion depth, and local work must be paid at every node in the recursion tree. Knowing only that a function calls itself is insufficient: one child of size n−1 behaves very differently from two children of size n/2, even if both functions are named `dfs` or `solve`.

blocks.text: Worst case is the maximum work over valid inputs of a fixed size; best case is the minimum. Average case is an expected value and therefore needs a stated probability distribution over inputs. Amortized analysis instead bounds the average cost across a sequence of operations, often deterministically: an occasional expensive array resize can be paid for by many cheap appends. It is not the same as assuming random inputs.

messages.text: Amortized bounds can be deterministic over every operation sequence.
